title: Numbers and counting
title_target: Siji, loro, telu… selawe, sèket, sewidak
goal: Count from one to a thousand, give your age, and deal with three surprises in Javanese numbers that you won't find in any other language you know: the *likur* series, *selawé* and *sèket*.
bekal: give your age and ask someone else's with *pira* / *pinten*

dialogs.title: Dialogue — Ngitung ing teras
dialogs.intro: Rini is counting the boarding house's shared cash on the porch. Dian sits down with her, and the conversation turns to age — a question that's perfectly normal in Java, not rude.

lines.speaker: Rini:
lines.text: Sedhéla, aku lagi ngitung. Siji, loro, telu… ah, kliru manèh.
lines.id: Hang on, I'm counting. One, two, three… argh, wrong again.
lines.literal: a-moment, I currently count. one, two, three… ah, wrong again.

lines.speaker: Rini:
lines.text: Dhuwit kas kos. Kudune ana rong atus sèket èwu.
lines.id: The house kitty. There should be two hundred and fifty thousand.
lines.literal: money cash boarding-house. should-the there-is two hundred fifty thousand.

lines.speaker: Rini:
lines.text: Kurang selawé èwu. Anak kos ing kéné ana sewelas.
lines.id: Twenty-five thousand short. There are eleven of us living here.
lines.literal: short twenty-five thousand. child boarding-house at here there-is eleven.

lines.speaker: Rini:
lines.text: Telu lagi mulih. Umurmu pira, Yan?
lines.id: Three have gone home. How old are you, Yan?
lines.literal: three currently go-home. age-your how-much, Yan?

lines.speaker: Rini:
lines.text: Padha. Aku uga rolikur, lair taun sangang puluh telu.
lines.id: Same. I'm twenty-two too, born in ninety-three.
lines.literal: same. I also twenty-two, born year ninety three.

lines.speaker: Dian:
lines.id: Javanese numbers are hard, aren't they?

lines.speaker: Rini:
lines.text: Sing angèl mung telu: likur, selawé, sèket. Liyané gampang.
lines.id: Only three are hard: likur, selawé, sèket. The rest are easy.
lines.literal: which hard only three: likur, selawé, sèket. other-the easy.

notes: **Kudune** means "should, is supposed to", from *kudu* (must) + the ending *-né*. *Kudu* itself is very common: *aku kudu lunga* (I have to go). Krama: *kedah*.

**Mung** means "only, just", krama *namung* or *namung kémawon*. It overlaps with *waé*, but *mung* goes **before** what it limits (*mung wolu*, only eight) while *waé* goes **after** (*wolu waé*, eight only).
**Kliru** means "wrong, mistaken" — a counting error or the wrong person. For "wrong" in the sense of guilty, use *salah*. Krama: *lepat*.

**Lair** (born) and **taun** (year) — Javanese shares a huge number of words like these with Indonesian, often with a dropped *h* or a shifted vowel (Indonesian *lahir*, *tahun*). If you know some Indonesian, spotting the pattern will speed you up enormously.

**Umurmu pira?** (How old are you?) is an everyday question in Java, asked of new acquaintances without any awkwardness. It isn't idle chat: the answer decides which title people will use for you and which speech level is right. The krama form is *yuswa panjenengan pinten?* — with *yuswa*, the honorific word for age.
**Sedhéla** means "a moment" (*sekedhap* in krama). It's *sedhéla* with **dh**, not plain *d* — and it's one of the words you'll say most often every day.

grammars.title: One to ten, two levels
body: The first ten numbers are the foundation of the whole system. Learn both columns as pairs from the start — don't do ngoko first and krama later.
after: Notice that **six to nine are the same** at both levels. You only need to learn the first five and ten twice.

grammars.title: Eleven to nineteen, and the famous likur series
body: Here Javanese differs from any language you probably know. The numbers 21–29 don't use "twenty" at all; they have their own series ending in ***-likur***. And in the middle of that series sits one word with no pattern whatsoever: **selawé** for 25.
after: **The *-likur* series exists only for 21–29.** After 29 the system goes back to normal: 31 is *telung puluh siji* (three tens one), not anything ending in *-likur*.
**Selawé (25)** is the word you'll hear most from this whole series, because it's used for money: *selawé èwu* = Rp25,000. Learn it before the rest.

In krama, many speakers keep the *-likur* series as it is, but the standard form uses *kalih dasa* + number: *kalih dasa setunggal* (21), *kalih dasa gangsal* (25). At A1, using ngoko *selawé* inside a krama sentence still sounds perfectly natural.

sections.title: Tens, hundreds, thousands — and the combining forms

blocks.text: To make tens, hundreds and thousands, the unit number first **changes shape** (a bit like *two* → *twen-* in English). The change is regular and only needs learning once.
After that, the tens hold one last surprise: **50 and 60 have names of their own** instead of being built.
Big numbers are built just like in English — largest to smallest, with no "and": *rong atus sèket èwu* (250,000), *telung èwu limang atus* (3,500), *sèket loro* (52).

blocks.title: Four things to memorize; the rest follows a pattern
items: These four are the whole difficulty of Javanese numbers. Every other number is built by the rules above.
More good news: in big cities, Javanese speakers themselves often switch to Indonesian numbers for large, complicated amounts. What stays in Javanese is small numbers and prices.

blocks.text: **Kapindho** (second) has one small oddity: *pindho* doesn't come from *loro* but from an old root related to Sanskrit *dwi* (two). It also appears in *ping pindho* (twice). Otherwise, order words are formed regularly with the prefix *ka-*.

blocks.title: Number practice that actually works
items: Count backwards from 30 to 20 out loud. The *-likur* series will feel strange exactly where it should, and that's what makes it stick.
Read every price you see today in Javanese: coffee, fuel, the balance on your screen. Numbers stick only through use, never through memorizing lists.
If you forget one mid-conversation, just say it in English or Indonesian and carry on. Young Javanese speakers mix like this every day.
There are eleven people living in this boarding house.
The money is only fifty thousand.
